subject: Mathematics

chapters.title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

cases.title: Heritage Walk on a Coordinate Map
source_sections: 1.4 Distance Between Two Points in the 2-D Plane
cases.passage: A town council prepares a coordinate map for a heritage walk. The school S is taken as the origin (0, 0). The library L is at (6, 8), the museum M is at (−6, 8), and the clinic C is at (6, 0). One unit on the coordinate grid represents 100 metres. Visitors may walk directly between two places when a straight path is available. Use the map and the distance between two points to answer the questions.

figure.caption: Figure 1: Coordinate map with grid lines one coordinate unit apart
figure.alt_text: A coordinate grid with grid lines one unit apart, S at the origin, L at 6 comma 8, M at minus 6 comma 8, and C at 6 comma 0. Each coordinate unit represents 100 metres.

questions.text: In which quadrant is the library L located?
How far is the clinic C from the y-axis, in metres?
Calculate the straight-line distances LM and MS. Give both answers in metres.

cases.title: Robot Route on a Game course
source_sections: 1.4 Distance Between Two Points in the 2-D Plane
cases.passage: A robot moves on a square game course marked as a coordinate plane. It starts at P(−4, 3), moves vertically to Q(−4, −5), and then moves horizontally to R(2, −5). It can also travel directly from P to R. Each unit on the course represents one metre. The programmer wants to compare the grid route P to Q to R with the direct route P to R.

figure.caption: Figure 2: Grid route PQR and direct route PR on a one-unit grid
figure.alt_text: A coordinate grid with grid lines one unit apart showing P at minus 4 comma 3, Q at minus 4 comma minus 5, and R at 2 comma minus 5, with segments PQ, QR, and PR. Each coordinate unit represents one metre.

questions.text: In which quadrant is point P located?
Find the length PQ.
Find the lengths of the grid route PQR and the direct route PR. Which route is shorter?
questions.answer: PQ + QR = 8 + 6 = 14 m. PR = √[(2 + 4)² + (−5 − 3)²] = √(36 + 64) = 10 m. The direct route is shorter by 4 m.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for direct route = 10 m and identifying it as shorter.

cases.title: Drone Inspection Route
source_sections: 1.4 Distance Between Two Points in the 2-D Plane
cases.passage: A drone inspects three solar towers. The control station W is at (2, 1), tower A is at (5, 5), and tower B is at (8, 1). Coordinates are measured in kilometres. The operator notices that the route from W to A and the route from A to B appear to have the same length. The distance formula can be used to check the observation.

questions.text: What is the perpendicular distance of A from the y-axis?
Calculate the distance WA.
Calculate AB and use the result to explain why triangle WAB is isosceles.
questions.answer: AB = √[(8 − 5)² + (1 − 5)²] = √25 = 5 km. Since WA = AB = 5 km, triangle WAB is isosceles.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for concluding WA = AB, so the triangle is isosceles.

cases.title: Growing Mosaic Border
cases.passage: An art club builds a sequence of square mosaics. At stage n, the border requires T(n) = 4n + 3 blue tiles. The coefficient 4 describes the fixed increase from one stage to the next, while 3 is the constant part of the rule. The club records the number of tiles before ordering material for a large display.

questions.text: What is the constant term of the linear polynomial T(n) = 4n + 3?
How many blue tiles are required at stage 12?
At which stage will the border require 75 blue tiles? Show the equation used.
questions.answer: 4n + 3 = 75, so 4n = 72 and n = 18. The border requires 75 tiles at stage 18.

cases.title: Water Tank with Linear Decay
cases.passage: A laboratory tank initially contains 240 litres of water. A pump removes water at a constant rate of 15 litres per hour. If t is the number of hours for which the pump runs, the volume remaining is V(t) = 240 − 15t litres. The rule is linear because the volume changes by the same amount during each hour.

questions.text: What does V(0) represent, and what is its value?
questions.answer: V(0) is the initial volume, equal to 240 litres.

questions.text: Find the volume remaining after 6 hours.
After how many hours will 90 litres remain? Also state the hourly rate of change of the volume.
questions.answer: 240 − 15t = 90 gives 15t = 150, so t = 10 hours. The rate of change is −15 litres per hour, meaning a decrease of 15 litres each hour.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for rate = −15 litres per hour with correct interpretation.

cases.title: Comparing Two Taxi Plans
cases.passage: Two taxi companies use linear fare rules. Company A charges A(d) = 50 + 12d rupees and Company B charges B(d) = 80 + 8d rupees, where d is the distance in kilometres. The fixed charge is represented by the constant term and the per-kilometre charge by the coefficient of d. A graph of the two rules shows where the fares become equal.

figure.caption: Figure 3: Fare graphs for Taxi A and Taxi B
figure.alt_text: A line graph of fare against distance. Taxi A starts at 50 and rises by 12 per kilometre. Taxi B starts at 80 and rises by 8 per kilometre. The lines meet at 7.5 kilometres and 140 rupees.

questions.text: Find Company A's fare for a journey of 5 km.
In the rule A(d), which quantity is the dependent variable?
questions.answer: The fare A(d) is the dependent variable.

questions.text: Find the distance at which the two companies charge the same fare, and calculate that fare.
questions.answer: 50 + 12d = 80 + 8d gives 4d = 30, so d = 7.5 km. The common fare is 50 + 12(7.5) = ₹140.

cases.title: Temperature Changes at a Hill Station
source_sections: 3.4 Filling the Spaces: Fractions and Rational Numbers
cases.passage: At sunrise, the temperature at a hill station was −4°C. By noon it rose by 7.5°C. During the afternoon it fell by 3.25°C. These changes can be represented by adding positive and negative rational numbers. The weather station records both the final temperature and the net change from sunrise.

questions.text: What was the temperature at noon?
What was the temperature after the afternoon fall?
Calculate the net change from sunrise to the final reading and verify it using the two recorded changes.
questions.answer: Final minus initial = 0.25 − (−4) = 4.25°C. Also, 7.5 + (−3.25) = 4.25°C, so the values agree.

cases.title: Ribbons of Rational Length
source_sections: 3.4 Filling the Spaces: Fractions and Rational Numbers
cases.passage: A craft teacher cuts three ribbons of lengths 3/4 m, 5/6 m, and 7/8 m. The class compares the rational lengths and then uses the average of two lengths to locate another rational number between them. All three pieces are cut from a roll that was initially 3 m long.

questions.text: Which of the three ribbon pieces is the longest?
Find the rational number obtained by averaging 3/4 and 5/6.
Find the total length used and the length remaining from the 3 m roll.

cases.title: Classifying Digital Number Displays
source_sections: 3.6 Real Numbers: Decimals and Cyclic Patterns
cases.passage: A digital exhibit displays four real numbers: A = 0.375, B = 0.272727..., C = √2, and D = 1.01001000100001..., where the number of zeros between successive 1s keeps increasing. The exhibit asks visitors to classify decimal expansions as terminating, non-terminating repeating, or non-terminating non-repeating.

questions.text: Which displayed number is a terminating decimal?
Which displayed number is non-terminating and repeating?
Classify C and D as rational or irrational, giving one reason for each classification.
questions.answer: C = √2 is irrational. D is also irrational because its decimal expansion neither terminates nor repeats a fixed block.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for correctly classifying √2 as irrational.
1 mark for classifying D as irrational with the non-terminating, non-repeating reason.

cases.title: Expanding a Square Courtyard
cases.passage: A square courtyard originally has side x metres. A 4 m wide extension is added along one side and another 4 m wide extension along the adjacent side, producing a larger square of side (x + 4) metres. The area model separates the new square into an x by x square, two rectangles of area 4x, and a 4 by 4 square.

figure.caption: Figure 4: Schematic area model for (x + 4)², not to scale
figure.alt_text: A schematic square of side x plus 4 divided into an x by x square, two x by 4 rectangles, and one 4 by 4 square. The drawing is not to scale because x is unspecified.

questions.text: Write the expanded area of the larger square.
Name the algebraic identity used in the expansion.
If x = 6 m, find the area of the larger courtyard and the increase over the original area.
questions.answer: Larger area = (6 + 4)² = 100 m². Original area = 6² = 36 m², so the increase is 64 m².

cases.title: Factoring a Rectangular Garden
source_sections: 4.3 Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions Using Identities
cases.passage: A rectangular garden has area x² + 7x + 12 square metres. To recover possible expressions for its length and breadth, the gardener looks for two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is 7. This converts the area polynomial into a product of two linear factors.

questions.text: Which two positive integers have product 12 and sum 7?
Factorise x² + 7x + 12.
For x = 5 m, find the garden's dimensions and perimeter.
questions.answer: Dimensions are x + 3 = 8 m and x + 4 = 9 m. Perimeter = 2(8 + 9) = 34 m.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for dimensions 8 m and 9 m.

cases.title: Square Frame and Difference of Squares
cases.passage: A square solar panel of side a metres has a smaller square opening of side b metres cut from it. The usable material has area a² − b² square metres. The manufacturer uses the difference-of-squares identity to calculate the area quickly from the sum and difference of the two side lengths.

questions.text: Factorise a² − b².
Find the usable area when a = 12 m and b = 8 m.
If a − b = 2 m and a + b = 18 m, find the usable area and the values of a and b.
questions.answer: Usable area = (a − b)(a + b) = 2 × 18 = 36 m². Solving a − b = 2 and a + b = 18 gives a = 10 m and b = 8 m.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for a = 10 m and b = 8 m.

chapters.title: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

cases.title: A Chord in a Circular Window
source_sections: 5.5 Midpoints and Perpendicular Bisectors of Chords
5.6 Distance of Chords from the Centre
cases.passage: A circular window has centre O and radius 10 cm. A supporting bar forms chord AB. The perpendicular OM from the centre to the chord is 6 cm long. A perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, so M is the midpoint of AB. Triangle OMA is right-angled at M.

figure.caption: Figure 5: Chord AB with OM perpendicular to AB
figure.alt_text: A circle with centre O, horizontal chord AB, midpoint M on the chord, and perpendicular segment OM. Radius OA is 10 centimetres and OM is 6 centimetres.

questions.text: What relation holds between AM and MB?
At which point is triangle OMA right-angled?
questions.answer: Triangle OMA is right-angled at M.

questions.text: Calculate the length of chord AB.
questions.answer: AM = √(OA² − OM²) = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm. Since M bisects AB, AB = 2 × 8 = 16 cm.

cases.title: Equal Chords in a Circular Stage
source_sections: 5.4 Chords and the Angles They Subtend
5.6 Distance of Chords from the Centre
cases.passage: Two equal lighting bars AB and CD are installed as chords of the same circular stage. Each chord is 5 m from the centre O, and the stage has radius 13 m. Equal chords of the same circle are equidistant from the centre and subtend equal angles at the centre. A perpendicular from O to either chord bisects it.

questions.text: How do the angles subtended by AB and CD at O compare?
What is the distance of chord CD from O?
Calculate the length of each chord.
questions.answer: Half-chord = √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 m. Therefore, each chord is 2 × 12 = 24 m long.

cases.title: Four Sensors on a Circular Track
cases.passage: Four sensors A, B, C, and D lie on the same circular track in that order. Chords AB, BC, CD, and DA form a cyclic quadrilateral. The measured angles are ∠BAD = 72° and ∠ABD = 45°. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and angles standing on the same chord are equal.

figure.caption: Figure 6: Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD
figure.alt_text: A circle containing four points A, B, C, and D joined to form a cyclic quadrilateral, with diagonal BD shown. The diagram is constructed so that angle BAD is 72 degrees and angle ABD is 45 degrees, and both angles are labelled.

questions.text: Find ∠BCD, the angle opposite ∠BAD.
Find ∠ACD if both ∠ABD and ∠ACD stand on chord AD.
Find ∠ADB and hence find ∠ACB, which stands on chord AB.
questions.answer: In triangle ABD, ∠ADB = 180° − 72° − 45° = 63°. Since ∠ADB and ∠ACB stand on chord AB, ∠ACB = 63°.

cases.title: Repairing a Circular Running Track
source_sections: 6.4 Length of an Arc of a Circle
6.10.1 Area of Sector of a Circle
cases.passage: A circular running track has radius 14 m. A 90° sector of the inner field is closed for repair. The school uses π = 22/7 for all calculations. The repair boundary includes the quarter-circle arc, and the grounds team also wants the area of the closed sector.

figure.caption: Figure 7: A 90 degree sector in a circle of radius 14 m
figure.alt_text: A circle of radius 14 metres with a shaded sector measuring 90 degrees.

questions.text: Find the circumference of the track.
Find the length of the 90° arc.
Find the area of the closed sector and the area of the remaining part of the circular field.
questions.answer: Sector area = 90/360 × 22/7 × 14² = 154 m². Total circle area = 616 m², so remaining area = 616 − 154 = 462 m².

cases.title: Grass for a Triangular Plot
cases.passage: A triangular plot has side lengths 13 m, 14 m, and 15 m. Since its height is not given directly, the landscape team uses Heron's formula. Grass is to be laid over the entire plot at ₹50 per square metre. The semiperimeter is denoted by s.

questions.text: Find the semiperimeter s of the plot.
Write the numerical expression under the square root in Heron's formula.
Find the area of the plot and the total cost of laying grass.

cases.title: A Stadium-Shaped Walking Path
cases.passage: A walking path is shaped like a rectangle 28 m long and 14 m wide, with a semicircle attached at each shorter end. Each semicircle has diameter 14 m, and together the two semicircles form one complete circle. Use π = 22/7. Only the outside boundary is counted when finding the perimeter.

figure.caption: Figure 8: Stadium shape formed by a rectangle and two semicircles
figure.alt_text: A rectangle 28 metres long and 14 metres wide with a semicircle of diameter 14 metres attached to each shorter side.

questions.text: What is the radius of each semicircular end?
What is the total length of the two straight parts of the boundary?
Calculate the complete outside perimeter of the path.
questions.answer: The two semicircles form a circle of radius 7 m, whose circumference is 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 m. Total perimeter = 56 + 44 = 100 m.

chapters.title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

cases.title: Testing a Die
cases.passage: Students roll a fair die 120 times. The observed frequencies for faces 1 to 6 are 18, 22, 19, 21, 17, and 23 respectively. Experimental probability is calculated from observed frequency, while theoretical probability for a fair die is based on six equally likely outcomes. The class compares the two types of probability.

questions.text: Find the experimental probability of obtaining a 6.
Find the theoretical probability of obtaining an even number.
Find the experimental probability of an even number and compare it with the theoretical probability.
questions.answer: Even outcomes occurred 22 + 21 + 23 = 66 times, so experimental P(even) = 66/120 = 0.55. The theoretical value is 0.50, so the experimental value is greater by 0.05.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for comparison with 0.50 and difference 0.05.

cases.title: Colour Spinner at a School Fair
cases.passage: A fair spinner is divided into eight equal sectors. Three sectors are red, two are blue, two are green, and one is yellow. Because the sectors are equal, each sector is equally likely. A colour event may contain one sector or several sectors, so its probability is the number of favourable sectors divided by eight.

figure.caption: Figure 9: Spinner with eight equal colour-labelled sectors
figure.alt_text: A circular spinner divided into eight equal sectors labelled R, R, R, B, B, G, G, and Y.

questions.text: Find the probability of landing on yellow.
Find the probability of not landing on red.
Blue and green are grouped as cool colours. Compare the probability of a cool colour with the probability of red.
questions.answer: P(cool) = (2 + 2)/8 = 4/8 = 1/2. P(red) = 3/8. A cool colour is more likely by 1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for stating cool is more likely by 1/8.

cases.title: Two-Coin Tree Diagram
cases.passage: Two fair coins are tossed one after the other. A tree diagram records H or T for the first toss and then H or T for the second toss. The four terminal outcomes are equally likely. The diagram can be used to identify events such as exactly one head or at least one head.

figure.caption: Figure 10: Tree diagram for two successive coin tosses
figure.alt_text: A probability tree branching from the first toss to H and T, and from each branch to H and T, ending at HH, HT, TH, and TT.

questions.text: Write the sample space for the experiment.
Find the probability of obtaining exactly one head.
questions.answer: The favourable outcomes are HT and TH, so P(exactly one head) = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.text: Find the probability of obtaining at least one head and explain how the tree diagram supports the result.
questions.answer: The outcomes with at least one head are HH, HT, and TH. Thus P(at least one head) = 3/4. The tree shows these as three of the four equally likely terminal branches.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for identifying HH, HT, and TH.
1 mark for probability = 3/4 with reference to three of four branches.

chapters.title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

cases.title: Seats in an Auditorium
cases.passage: An auditorium has 18 seats in the first row. Each new row has four more seats than the row before it. The numbers of seats form the arithmetic progression 18, 22, 26, 30, and so on. The first term is 18 and the common difference is 4.

questions.text: What is the common difference of the progression?
How many seats are in the fifth row?
Write an explicit rule for the number of seats in row n and use it to find the number of seats in row 20.

cases.title: Branching Plant Pattern
cases.passage: A computer model begins with 2 branches at Stage 1. At every new stage, each branch is replaced by three branches, so the total number of branches triples and the counts are 2, 6, 18, 54, and so on. The sequence is a geometric progression because the ratio of each term to the preceding term is constant.

questions.text: What is the common ratio of the progression?
How many branches are present at Stage 4?
Write an explicit rule for the number of branches at Stage n and use it to find the Stage 5 count.

cases.title: Triangular Tile Displays
source_sections: 8.5 Sum of the First n Natural Numbers
cases.passage: An exhibition arranges circular tiles in triangular patterns. Stage 1 has 1 tile, Stage 2 has 3 tiles, Stage 3 has 6 tiles, and Stage 4 has 10 tiles. At Stage n, the number of tiles is the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n, so Tₙ = n(n + 1)/2. Each new stage adds one more row than the previous stage.

figure.caption: Figure 11: The first four triangular tile patterns
figure.alt_text: Four triangular dot patterns containing 1, 3, 6, and 10 tiles at Stages 1, 2, 3, and 4.

questions.text: How many tiles are in Stage 5?
How many new tiles are added when moving from Stage 4 to Stage 5?
Find the number of tiles in Stage 10 and state the recursive relation connecting consecutive triangular numbers.
questions.answer: T₁₀ = 10 × 11/2 = 55. The recursive relation is Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + n, with T₁ = 1.
marking_scheme: 1 mark for Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + n with initial term.
